extracted.intended_audience: legislators, jurists, political philosophers, and students of political law
extracted.subtask_description: Normative principles and practical recommendations about justice, punishments, and judicial organization across different forms of government (despotism, monarchy, republic). Geared toward designing laws and institutional arrangements that restrain abuse and promote public order and virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign must not be judge in monarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: «Dans les États despotiques, le prince peut juger lui-même. Il ne le peut dans les monarchies: la constitution serait détruite... » — Le prince qui juge serait à la fois juge et partie.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons: destroys constitution and intermediary powers, creates conflict of interest (prince = partie qui poursuit), removes the sovereign's distinctive power to grant grace, and invites extortion by courtiers. Historical examples cited: Louis XIII's attempt, emperors Claude, Néron, Arcadius, Justinian; use legislative limits instead (see Rome).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ministers should not adjudicate in monarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: «C'est encore un grand inconvénient dans la monarchie que les ministres du prince jugent eux-mêmes les affaires contentieuses.»
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasoning: council of the monarch should be small and passionate about policy; tribunals require many judges with sang-froid and impartiality. Mixing roles leads to contradiction between conseil du monarque and tribunaux and risks politicization of judicial decisions. Avoid ministrial adjudication of fiscal and contentieux matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single magistrate (magistrat unique) only in despotism
rubrics_metrics.description: «Un tel magistrat ne peut avoir lieu que dans le gouvernement despotique.»
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sole judge invites abuse (examples: Appius, decemvirs). Institutional design should avoid concentrating judicial power in one person except under despotic regimes; prefer multi-member tribunals for checks and impartiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fix legal forms and present a single fact to popular juries
rubrics_metrics.description: Romans introduced 'formules d'actions' to direct each affair by the action appropriate to it so that the people would always have a single state of the question before them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the people judge (as in a republic), the issue presented must be precise and immutable during deliberation so the multitude can decide on a single concrete fact (absolve, condemn, remit). Avoid shifting states of question in large affairs. Where judges deliberate (monarchy), more discretionary formulas (actions 'de bonne foi') may be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal protections for accused: allow exile and prevent popular confiscation
rubrics_metrics.description: Roman legislators allowed the accused to go into exile before judgment and consecrated the goods of the condemned so the people would not have their confiscation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design procedural safeguards that limit popular temptation to confiscate and punish precipitously: permit voluntary exile to avoid mob punishment; allocate confiscated goods so the populace does not profit, reducing incentives for unjust prosecutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay and appellate review in capital or passionate cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Solon required that the Areopagus review affairs and, if an accused seemed unjustly absous or condemned, could reprosecute or stop execution; 'Il sera bon de mettre quelque lenteur... afin que le peuple puisse se calmer et juger de sang-froid.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutionalize cooling-off periods and review mechanisms (stay of execution, review by respected magistrature) especially where the accused is imprisoned or passions run high, to prevent summary or vindictive judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit private delation; use a public prosecutor
rubrics_metrics.description: Private denunciations (delateurs) arise where citizens may accuse others freely; better to have the prince prepose an officer in each tribunal to prosecute in his name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Centralize prosecution to a public officer to avoid a crowd of opportunistic accusers who seek favor and fortune via prosecutions. Include accountability: if the public prosecutor abuses his office, require him to name his dénonciateur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Severity of penalties should fit the government type
rubrics_metrics.description: «La sévérité des peines convient mieux au gouvernement despotique, dont le principe est la terreur, qu'à la monarchie et à la république, qui ont pour ressort l'honneur et la vertu.»
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despotisms rely on terror and thus use harsher punishments; moderate governments should emphasize honor, virtue, and prevention. Legislators in moderate states should avoid excessive corporal punishments and prefer measures that cultivate morals and social restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: In moderate states prioritize prevention and moral formation over harsh punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: «Un bon législateur s'attachera moins à punir les crimes qu'à les prévenir; il s'appliquera plus à donner des mœurs qu'à infliger des supplices.»
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design laws that shape customs, reward virtue, and use education/religion/honor as tools of prevention rather than relying primarily on severe penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: When a people is virtuous, few legal penalties are needed
rubrics_metrics.description: «Que lorsqu'un peuple est vertueux, il faut peu de peines.» — The Roman example: many penalties were removed without harming public order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that social virtue reduces need for coercive penalties; laws should support and not erode civic probity. Observe historical examples (Rome) where removal of harsh penalties did not produce disorder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid extreme or escalating punishments that erode government legitimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive punishments make governments corrupt and desensitize subjects; examples include wheel torture temporarily stopping highway robbery, then crimes resumed; extreme penalties breed habituation and the need for ever greater severity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on extreme punishments to temporarily suppress crimes; such measures exhaust the moral authority of the government and lead to cycles of increasing cruelty and eventual despotism or revolution (examples from history and China/Japan).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use shame/infamy as an effective punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: «Suivons la nature, qui a donné aux hommes la honte comme leur fléau; et que la plus grande partie de la peine soit l'infamie de la souffrir.»
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage social disgrace and loss of honor as lasting sanctions that align with human psychology, instead of defaulting to bodily torture or excessive corporal penalties. Combine infamy with pecuniary penalties when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion between crimes and penalties (juste proportion)
rubrics_metrics.description: «Il est essentiel que les peines aient de l'harmonie entre elles...» — punishments must be proportionate to the gravity of offenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid equating theft and murder with identical penalties; calibrate sanctions so they discourage greater harms more effectively. Use gradation and differential consequences (and hope for grace) to deter worse crimes. Historical mismatches (e.g., disproportionate treatment of calumny vs lèse-majesté) are warnings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use hope of mercy and differentiated prospects (e.g., transportation) to reduce severe crimes
rubrics_metrics.description: When penalties for different crimes are identical, provide differences in hope of grace (e.g., transportation for thieves in England) so people may avoid escalating to more violent crimes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incentivize less harmful criminal choices by offering more lenient post-conviction prospects for lesser crimes; the system of pardons and commutations can reduce the incidence of more serious offences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Torture/question of criminals is unnecessary and morally objectionable
rubrics_metrics.description: «La question contre les criminels n'est pas dans un cas forcé... Nous voyons aujourd'hui une nation très bien policée la rejeter...» — the practice can be rejected without disadvantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given moral objections and effective alternatives (witness rules, evidentiary standards), avoid using torture; it may befit despotic systems but conflicts with nature and justice. Follow philosophic and legal critiques against the practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance pecuniary and corporal penalties; seek a middle course
rubrics_metrics.description: Germans preferred pecuniary penalties; Japanese reject pecuniary fines; a wise legislator takes the juste milieu and does not impose only fines nor only corporal punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design penalties proportionate to fortunes (fines scaled to means) and combine with infamy or non-lethal sanctions. Avoid systemic bias where the rich can buy impunity or where fines are ineffective because they are too light relative to wealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temper the law of talion in moderate states
rubrics_metrics.description: «Les États despotiques... usent beaucoup de la loi du talion; les États modérés la reçoivent quelquefois: mais... les autres lui donnent presque toujours des tempéraments.»
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Talion may function in simple or despotic systems; moderate regimes should allow commutations or monetary compensation (as under the Douze Tables) and avoid rigid literal retaliation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective/familial punishment is characteristic of despotism and unjust
rubrics_metrics.description: «On punit à la Chine les pères pour les fautes de leurs enfants... Ceci est encore tiré des idées despotiques.»
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid punishing parents for children's crimes; prefer individual responsibility and social sanctions like shame rather than collective capital punishment which is despotic and undermines honor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use clemency (grace) as an instrument of monarchic government
rubrics_metrics.description: «La clémence est la qualité distinctive des monarques... Les monarques ont tant à gagner par la clémence... »
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clemency builds love, glory, and political advantage for monarchs, and functions as an alternative to harsh punishment especially for great persons; exercise pardons judiciously, distinguishing clemency from weakness, and be mindful of dangers when mercy undermines authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for social rank and honor when prescribing penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: In ancient French laws and in monarchies penalties differ by social condition: pecuniary penalties affect non-nobles differently; nobles more often suffer loss of honor than corporal punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When legislating, consider how punishments interact with social honor structures; in some systems disgrace may be more significant than bodily punishment for elites. Design sanctions that are meaningful across social strata without producing gross inequalities that corrode legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid legislating harsh new penalties as a first resort to correct evils
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislators who seek quick corrections by severe penalties often fail to foresee long-term harms: 'Lorsque le mal est une fois corrigé, on ne voit plus que la dureté du législateur; mais il reste un vice...'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer enforcing existing laws and using moderate, well-considered reforms. Sudden imposition of extreme punishments can corrupt public morals and produce worse social vices.
